questions.subject: histology
questions.title: Epithelia: layers, shape and function
questions.prompt: A lining has nuclei at different heights. What additional observation best distinguishes pseudostratified from stratified epithelium?

options.text: Trace whether every cell reaches the basement membrane.
options.explanation: In pseudostratified epithelium all cells reach the basement membrane, although some do not reach the lumen; true stratification includes cells above the basal layer.

options.text: Count all nuclei seen in the section, regardless of cell boundaries.
options.explanation: Nuclear height or the total number of nuclear profiles alone cannot establish the number of epithelial layers.

options.text: Check whether the superficial cells are taller than they are wide.
options.explanation: Surface-cell shape helps name an epithelium, but columnar cells can occur in both arrangements.

questions.subject: histology
questions.title: Epithelia: layers, shape and function
questions.prompt: A model exchange surface changes from one thin cell layer to several layers. With other variables fixed, what is the most direct consequence?

options.text: Diffusion becomes faster because there are more cells.
options.explanation: Adding layers increases the diffusion path; cell number alone does not improve passive exchange.

options.text: The diffusion path increases, making passive exchange slower.
options.explanation: A thin barrier shortens the path for diffusion. Several layers may help resist abrasion but impose a longer exchange path.

options.text: Transport is unchanged as long as the surface area is unchanged.
options.explanation: Diffusion depends on barrier thickness as well as area and the concentration or partial-pressure gradient.

questions.subject: biochemistry
questions.title: Amino-acid nitrogen and urea
questions.prompt: Why can transferring an amino group to glutamate not, by itself, complete nitrogen disposal?

options.text: The nitrogen has changed carrier but still needs a route to elimination.
options.explanation: Transamination redistributes nitrogen. The amino nitrogen must still be processed and ultimately excreted; the carbon skeleton follows its own metabolic fate.

options.text: Transamination always converts the amino nitrogen directly into urea.
options.explanation: Urea formation requires the urea-cycle reactions. An amino-group transfer is not the complete disposal pathway.

options.text: Once nitrogen reaches glutamate it cannot enter another pathway.
options.explanation: Glutamate collects and transfers nitrogen; it is a metabolic intermediate rather than a permanent endpoint.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.title: Predict a renal circuit response
questions.prompt: In the fixed-pressure two-resistor model, double efferent resistance while keeping afferent resistance at 1. What happens relative to baseline?

options.text: Flow falls and glomerular pressure rises.
options.explanation: Total resistance increases, lowering flow. A larger share of the fixed pressure drop is across the efferent resistance, raising pressure upstream of it. This circuit does not calculate GFR.

options.text: Flow and glomerular pressure both fall.
options.explanation: Flow falls, but efferent resistance is downstream of the glomerular node; pressure at that node rises in this fixed-pressure model.

options.text: Flow rises because glomerular pressure rises.
options.explanation: Pressure at an intermediate point is not the same as flow through the circuit. Total resistance has increased.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.title: Predict a renal circuit response
questions.prompt: Now double only afferent resistance. Which prediction follows from the same model?

options.text: Flow falls but glomerular pressure rises.
options.explanation: That was the downstream-resistance manipulation. Increasing upstream resistance lowers pressure at the glomerular node.

options.text: Flow and glomerular pressure both fall.
options.explanation: The total resistance rises and more of the pressure drop occurs before the glomerular node. This is a circuit prediction, not a clinical GFR estimate.

options.text: Flow is unchanged because arterial pressure is fixed.
options.explanation: A fixed driving pressure does not fix flow when total resistance changes.

questions.subject: histology
questions.title: Real section A
questions.prompt: Which classification best describes the lining of the large open tubule in section A?

options.text: Simple cuboidal epithelium
options.explanation: The lining forms one layer of cells with roughly similar height and width. Follow a single tubule wall; nearby tubules are separate structures, not extra epithelial layers.

options.text: Stratified cuboidal epithelium
options.explanation: Several adjacent tubules can mimic layers. A stratified epithelium has multiple layers within one lining between its basal boundary and free surface.

options.text: Simple squamous epithelium
options.explanation: Squamous cells are flattened. These tubular cells have appreciable cytoplasm around rounded nuclear profiles.

questions.subject: histology
questions.title: Transfer section B
questions.prompt: How should the thick lining facing the broad pale space in section B be classified?

options.text: Simple columnar epithelium
options.explanation: One layer of tall cells would connect the basal boundary to the surface. This lining contains many cell layers.

options.text: Pseudostratified columnar epithelium
options.explanation: Uneven nuclear heights alone do not make an epithelium stratified. Here the tissue has distinct stacked layers with flattening toward the free surface.

options.text: Stratified squamous epithelium
options.explanation: Multiple layers lie between the basal boundary and the free surface. Superficial cells flatten, so classification uses the surface cells rather than the deeper rounded cells.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.title: Volume V: trace a limb nerve through the plexus
questions.prompt: In a simplified plexus map, trace a C5 fibre into the axillary nerve. Which route fits?

options.text: Upper trunk → posterior division → posterior cord
options.explanation: C5 contributes to the upper trunk; its posterior division contributes to the posterior cord, from which the axillary nerve arises.

options.text: Upper trunk → anterior division → lateral cord
options.explanation: The upper trunk is correct, but its anterior division contributes to the lateral cord, not the cord giving rise to the axillary nerve.

options.text: Lower trunk → posterior division → posterior cord
options.explanation: The cord fits, but the usual lower trunk combines C8–T1 rather than C5.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.title: Volume V: trace a limb nerve through the plexus
questions.prompt: A model shows the three cords beside an artery deep to pectoralis minor. What identifies the landmark used to name the cords?

options.text: The axillary artery before it reaches pectoralis minor
options.explanation: That is the first part. Cord names refer to their relations to the second part.

options.text: The second part of the axillary artery
options.explanation: Pectoralis minor divides the artery into parts; the second part lies deep to the muscle and defines the cord names.

options.text: The brachial artery below teres major
options.explanation: This is distal to the axillary artery and is not the landmark defining the cord names.

questions.title: Histology Foundations: The Four Basic Tissues
questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: A superficial injury removes an epithelial lining while deeper smooth muscle remains intact. Which immediate functional loss follows most directly from the tissue that was removed?

options.text: All active force generation in the deeper muscle is abolished
options.explanation: The scenario preserves the deeper muscle. Loss of epithelial cells does not by itself establish loss of all muscle contraction.

options.text: The continuous protective barrier is disrupted
options.explanation: Epithelial continuity and cell junctions help maintain a barrier. Removing the lining exposes underlying tissue even when deeper contractile cells remain.

options.text: The extracellular collagen necessarily disappears from the supporting tissue
options.explanation: Collagen belongs to the supporting matrix. Its disappearance is not implied by selective removal of the epithelial layer.

questions.title: Histology Foundations: The Four Basic Tissues
questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: An unknown pink bundle has sparse flattened nuclei between abundant parallel extracellular fibres. No striations are seen. Which interpretation is best supported?

options.text: Dense regular connective tissue, because matrix dominates over cells
options.explanation: Abundant aligned extracellular collagen with relatively sparse flattened fibroblast nuclei supports dense regular connective tissue such as tendon. This uses positive architectural clues.

options.text: Smooth muscle, because absent striations identify a non-striated contractile bundle
options.explanation: Absent striations are not specific to smooth muscle. The positive findings here are abundant extracellular fibres and sparse flattened nuclei, which favour dense regular connective tissue.

options.text: Skeletal muscle cut obliquely, because orientation can conceal its striations
options.explanation: An oblique cut can obscure striations, but it does not explain a field dominated by extracellular collagen with sparse flattened nuclei. The stated architecture supports connective tissue.

questions.title: Histology Foundations: The Four Basic Tissues
questions.subject: histology
questions.prompt: Selective myelin injury affects a peripheral nerve while its axons initially remain intact. Which functional prediction and glial-cell attribution are best supported?

options.text: Conduction may slow or fail, and the affected myelin was formed by oligodendrocytes
options.explanation: The functional prediction is plausible, but the cell attribution is incorrect. Oligodendrocytes form CNS myelin; the question specifies a peripheral nerve.

options.text: Conduction must remain normal because the axons are still present
options.explanation: Axonal continuity does not guarantee normal conduction. Damage to insulating myelin can impair action-potential propagation even while the axon is initially intact.

options.text: Conduction may slow or fail, and the affected myelin was formed by Schwann cells
options.explanation: PNS myelin comes from Schwann cells and supports efficient action-potential propagation. This predicts a functional disturbance without assuming the whole neuron has died.

questions.title: Anatomy Foundations: Position, Planes and Organisation
questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: A hypothetical teaching image is a transverse section viewed from the feet towards the head, with anterior at the top. A marker is in the upper-left part of the display. Which description follows from this orientation?

options.text: Patient’s left and posterior
options.explanation: This reverses both supplied orientation cues. The patient’s left appears on the display’s right, and posterior is at the bottom.

options.text: Patient’s right and anterior
options.explanation: Under the stated viewing convention, display-left corresponds to the patient’s right. The top of this image is explicitly labelled anterior.

options.text: Patient’s right and superior within the section
options.explanation: The patient’s side is correct, but superior is perpendicular to a transverse section. The top of this display is anterior, not superior.

questions.title: Anatomy Foundations: Position, Planes and Organisation
questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: A hypothetical report describes fluid between the right visceral and parietal pleura. Which interpretation is anatomically justified?

options.text: Fluid is inside the right main bronchus
options.explanation: A bronchial lumen is within an airway. The report specifies a space outside the lung surface between pleural layers.

options.text: Fluid is in the pericardial cavity
options.explanation: The pericardial cavity is between serous pericardial layers, not pleural layers. The report identifies different boundaries.

options.text: Fluid occupies the right pleural cavity
options.explanation: The two named pleural surfaces define this space. This locates the fluid without establishing its cause or prescribing treatment.

questions.title: Anatomy Foundations: Position, Planes and Organisation
questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: A hypothetical superficial mark lies on the anterior right forearm, closer to the wrist than to the elbow. Which statement remains justified when the person turns the palm down?

options.text: The mark remains on the anatomical anterior surface of the right forearm
options.explanation: Rotating the limb changes its displayed orientation, not the established anatomical name of its surface or its side.

options.text: The mark becomes posterior because it now faces away from the viewer
options.explanation: The viewer’s changing position cannot rename anatomical surfaces. Use the reference position to describe the mark consistently.

options.text: The mark proves an underlying nerve injury
options.explanation: Surface location alone does not establish damage to a deep nerve. Depth, function and additional observations would be needed.

questions.title: Anatomy Foundations: Position, Planes and Organisation
questions.subject: anatomy
questions.prompt: In a simplified stomach-wall model, the epithelial lining remains intact while smooth-muscle contraction is reduced. Which function is most directly affected by the specified change?

options.text: The ability of the lining to form an epithelial barrier must be completely lost
options.explanation: Reduced muscle contraction does not itself establish epithelial destruction. The stem explicitly preserves the lining.

options.text: Mechanical mixing of the luminal contents
options.explanation: Smooth-muscle contraction contributes to mixing and propulsion. This prediction follows from the affected tissue’s function without assuming that every tissue has failed.

options.text: Every nervous signal in the organ must cease
options.explanation: The question identifies a muscle change, not loss of all nervous tissue. This conclusion goes beyond the supplied evidence.

questions.title: Physiology Foundations: Membrane Transport and Resting Potential
questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: In a teaching model, the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase is inhibited while Na⁺ leaks continue. After the Na⁺ gradient weakens, what happens to the energy available for Na⁺-coupled glucose uptake?

options.text: It increases because the cotransporter starts hydrolysing ATP.
options.explanation: The cotransporter does not become an ATPase when the separate pump is inhibited.

options.text: It is unchanged because a protein transporter needs no gradient.
options.explanation: Secondary active transport depends on the coupled electrochemical gradient, not simply the presence of a protein.

options.text: It decreases because the downhill Na⁺ movement supplies less energy.
options.explanation: Weakening the Na⁺ electrochemical gradient reduces the driving force available to support uphill glucose transport.

questions.title: Physiology Foundations: Membrane Transport and Resting Potential
questions.subject: physiology
questions.prompt: A model membrane is permeable only to K⁺. Intracellular K⁺ stays fixed while extracellular K⁺ increases but remains below the intracellular concentration. What happens to the K⁺ equilibrium potential?

options.text: It becomes more negative.
options.explanation: Raising outside K⁺ reduces the outward concentration gradient; less negative voltage is needed to oppose it.

options.text: It becomes less negative.
options.explanation: The outside-to-inside K⁺ concentration ratio increases, shifting the K⁺ equilibrium potential in the positive direction.

options.text: It is unchanged because K⁺ is not actively transported through the channel.
options.explanation: The equilibrium potential depends on the concentration ratio even though movement through the channel is passive.

questions.title: Biochemistry Foundations: Enzymes, Kinetics and Regulation
questions.subject: biochemistry
questions.prompt: Under ideal reversible competitive inhibition, the active enzyme amount and other conditions stay fixed. Which pattern is predicted?

options.text: Higher apparent Km with unchanged Vmax.
options.explanation: More substrate is needed for half the limiting rate, but sufficient substrate can still approach the same Vmax.

options.text: Lower Vmax with unchanged apparent Km in every case.
options.explanation: This is the ideal pure non-competitive pattern, not the competitive model specified in the question.

options.text: Lower apparent Km with higher Vmax.
options.explanation: Competition does not increase catalytic capacity or reduce the substrate requirement in this model.

questions.title: Biochemistry Foundations: Enzymes, Kinetics and Regulation
questions.subject: biochemistry
questions.prompt: A hypothetical Michaelis–Menten assay has Vmax = 60 µmol/min and Km = 3 mmol/L. At [S] = 3 mmol/L, what is the initial rate?

options.text: 60 µmol/min
options.explanation: Vmax is the limiting rate approached at high substrate, not the rate when [S] equals Km.

options.text: 30 mmol/L
options.explanation: The numerical half is correct, but this is a concentration unit rather than a rate.

options.text: 30 µmol/min
options.explanation: At [S] = Km, v = Vmax/2 = 30 µmol/min; the answer must retain rate units.

questions.title: Genetics Foundations: Genome, Inheritance and Gene Expression
questions.subject: genetics
questions.prompt: In an Aa × Aa autosomal recessive cross, assume AA and Aa are unaffected and aa is affected. Before knowing the phenotype, what is the probability of an Aa carrier child?

options.explanation: One of the four combinations is AA and one is aa, but two are heterozygous carriers.
Aa and aA are the two heterozygous outcomes among four equally likely combinations, giving 1/2.

options.text: Two thirds
options.explanation: Two thirds is the carrier probability conditional on an unaffected child in this model. That condition has not been supplied.

questions.title: Genetics Foundations: Genome, Inheritance and Gene Expression
questions.subject: genetics
questions.prompt: Two cell types contain the same intact gene, but one has much less of its mRNA. Which conclusion is justified by these observations alone?

options.text: RNA abundance differs; the gene need not be absent from either cell.
options.explanation: Different transcription or RNA stability can change mRNA abundance even when the DNA sequence is present in both cells.

options.text: The cell with less mRNA must have lost the chromosome.
options.explanation: The question states that the same intact gene is present; mRNA abundance alone does not show chromosome loss.

options.text: Both cells must contain equal amounts of functional protein.
options.explanation: DNA presence does not fix RNA or protein abundance, and function also depends on later processing and regulation.

questions.title: Biophysics Foundations: Diffusion, Osmosis and Membranes
questions.subject: biophysics
questions.prompt: Two compartments have equal initial hydrostatic pressure. A membrane passes water but not the dissolved solute. The right side has more solute particles per litre. What is the initial net water movement?

options.text: From right to left
options.explanation: That direction would increase the initial osmotic imbalance under the stated equal-pressure conditions.

options.text: No net movement because solute cannot cross
options.explanation: Solute impermeability does not prevent water movement; the membrane is explicitly permeable to water.

options.text: From left to right
options.explanation: Water initially moves towards the more concentrated impermeant-solute compartment when initial hydrostatic pressures are equal.

questions.title: Biophysics Foundations: Diffusion, Osmosis and Membranes
questions.subject: biophysics
questions.prompt: A model cell and bath initially have equal total osmolarity. The bath solute can enter the cell. Is unchanged cell volume guaranteed over time?

options.text: Yes, equal osmolarity always means equal tonicity.
options.explanation: Equal total particle concentration does not account for solute permeability or redistribution over time.

options.text: No; solute permeability and redistribution must also be considered.
options.explanation: A permeating solute can alter the effective osmotic gradient, so equal initial osmolarity does not guarantee stable cell volume.

options.text: Yes, provided diffusion uses no ATP.
options.explanation: Whether ATP is used does not determine tonicity; passive solute entry can still alter water balance.
